==Problem==
Joey and Chloe and their daughter Zoe all have the same birthday. Joey is <math>1</math> year older than Chloe, and Zoe is exactly <math>1</math> year old today. Today is the first of the <math>9</math> birthdays on which Chloe's age will be an integral multiple of Zoe's age. What will be the sum of the two digits of Joey's age the next time his age is a multiple of Zoe's age?

<math>
\textbf{(A) }7 \qquad
\textbf{(B) }8 \qquad
\textbf{(C) }9 \qquad
\textbf{(D) }10 \qquad
\textbf{(E) }11 \qquad
</math>

==Solution 1==
Suppose that Chloe is <math>c</math> years old today, so Joey is <math>c+1</math> years old today. After <math>n</math> years, Chloe and Zoe will be <math>n+c</math> and <math>n+1</math> years old, respectively. We are given that <cmath>\frac{n+c}{n+1}=1+\frac{c-1}{n+1}</cmath> is an integer for <math>9</math> nonnegative integers <math>n.</math> It follows that <math>c-1</math> has <math>9</math> positive divisors. The prime factorization of <math>c-1</math> is either <math>p^8</math> or <math>p^2q^2.</math> Since <math>c-1<100,</math> the only possibility is <math>c-1=2^2\cdot3^2=36,</math> from which <math>c=37.</math> We conclude that Joey is <math>c+1=38</math> years old today.

Suppose that Joey's age is a multiple of Zoe's age after <math>k</math> years, in which Joey and Zoe will be <math>k+38</math> and <math>k+1</math> years old, respectively. We are given that <cmath>\frac{k+38}{k+1}=1+\frac{37}{k+1}</cmath> is an integer for some positive integer <math>k.</math> It follows that <math>37</math> is divisible by <math>k+1,</math> so the only possibility is <math>k=36.</math> We conclude that Joey will be <math>k+38=74</math> years old then, from which the answer is <math>7+4=\boxed{\textbf{(E) }11}.</math>

==Solution 2==
Let Joey's age be <math>j</math>, Chloe's age be <math>c</math>, and we know that Zoe's age is <math>1</math>. 

We know that there must be <math>9</math> values <math>k\in\mathbb{Z}</math> such that <math>c+k=a(1+k)</math> where <math>a</math> is an integer.

Therefore, <math>c-1+(1+k)=a(1+k)</math> and <math>c-1=(1+k)(a-1)</math>. Therefore, we know that, as there are <math>9</math> solutions for <math>k</math>, there must be <math>9</math> solutions for <math>c-1</math>. We know that this must be a perfect square. Testing perfect squares, we see that <math>c-1=36</math>, so <math>c=37</math>. Therefore, <math>j=38</math>. Now, since <math>j-1=37</math>, by similar logic, <math>37=(1+k)(a-1)</math>, so <math>k=36</math> and Joey will be <math>38+36=74</math> and the sum of the digits is <math>\boxed{\textbf{(E) }11}</math>.

==Solution 3 ==

Let Chloe's age be <imath>c</imath> so that Zoey is 1. Then, if <imath>n</imath> years pass, we have that again <imath>c+n \equiv 0 \pmod{n+1}</imath> from which <imath>c \equiv 1 \pmod{n+1}</imath> thus <imath>c - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{n+1}</imath>. Hence, <imath>c-1</imath> has 9 divisors. Assuming no human lives past a century, it is given that only numbers of the form <imath>p^2q^2</imath> work. Taking minimality, <imath>p = 2, q = 3</imath> from which <imath>c-1 = 36 \implies c = 37</imath>. Hence, Joey is 38. Now, if after some <imath>k</imath> years Joey is a multiple of Zoe, we can just apply the same process as before. In other words, <imath>38+k \equiv 0 \pmod{1+k}</imath> hence <imath>38 \equiv 1 \pmod{1+k}</imath>, and thus <imath>37 \equiv 0 \pmod{1+k}</imath>. The only integer multiples of 37 is 1 and 37, but they wish for the next integral multiple, which is when Zoe is 38 years and Joey is 74, whose sum is <imath>\boxed{11}</imath>.

== Solution 4 ==

Here's a different way of stating Solution 2:

If a number is a multiple of both Chloe's age and Zoe's age, then it is a multiple of their difference. Since the difference between their ages does not change, then that means the difference between their ages has <math>9</math> factors. Therefore, the difference between Chloe and Zoe's age is <math>36</math>, so Chloe is <math>37</math>, and Joey is <math>38</math>. The common factor that will divide both of their ages is <math>37</math>, so Joey will be <math>74</math>. The answer is <math>7 + 4 =  \boxed{\textbf{(E) }11}</math>.

==Solution 5==
Similar approach to above, just explained less concisely and more in terms of the problem (less algebraic).

Let <imath>C+n</imath> denote Chloe's age, <imath>J+n</imath> denote Joey's age, and <imath>Z+n</imath> denote Zoe's age, where <imath>n</imath> is the number of years from now. We are told that <imath>C+n</imath> is a multiple of <imath>Z+n</imath> exactly nine times. Because <imath>Z+n</imath> is <imath>1</imath> at <imath>n=0</imath> and will increase until greater than <imath>C-Z</imath>, it will hit every natural number less than <imath>C-Z</imath>, including every factor of <imath>C-Z</imath>. For <imath>C+n</imath> to be an integral multiple of <imath>Z+n</imath>, the difference <imath>C-Z</imath> must also be a multiple of <imath>Z</imath>, which happens if <imath>Z</imath> is a factor of <imath>C-Z</imath>. Therefore, <imath>C-Z</imath> has nine factors. The smallest number that has nine positive factors is <imath>2^23^2=36</imath> . (We want it to be small so that Joey will not have reached three digits of age before his age is a multiple of Zoe's.) We also know <imath>Z=1</imath> and <imath>J=C+1</imath>. Thus,
<cmath>\begin{align*}
C-Z&=36, \\
J-Z&=37.
\end{align*}</cmath>
By our above logic, the next time <imath>J-Z</imath> is a multiple of <imath>Z+n</imath> will occur when <imath>Z+n</imath> is a factor of <imath>J-Z</imath>. Because <imath>37</imath> is prime, the next time this happens is at <imath>Z+n=37</imath>, when <imath>J+n=74</imath>. The answer is <imath>7+4=\boxed{\textbf{(E) }11}</imath>.

==Solution 6 (Number Theory+Logic)==

Let Joeys current age be <imath>J</imath>, Chloe's current age be <imath>C</imath>, Zoe's current age be <imath>Z</imath>, and <imath>C-Z=C-1=K</imath>. This gives <imath>C=1+K</imath> and <imath>J=2+K</imath>. 
After <imath>t</imath> years, Zoe will be <imath>Z+t=t+1</imath> years old and Chloe will be <imath>C+t</imath> years old. 
Chloe's age is an integral multiple of Zoe's age when <imath>Z+t|C+t</imath>. By the Divisibility of Differences rule (which is a unique case of the linear combination property of divisibility), <imath>t+1|C+t-(t+1)</imath>-><imath>t+1|C-1</imath>-><imath>t+1=K</imath>.

<imath>K</imath> must have exactly <imath>9</imath> positive integer factors, since there are precisely <imath>9</imath> values of <imath>t</imath> for which Zoe's age is a factor of Chloe's age. The smallest number with this property is <imath>2^2 \times 3^2=36</imath>. We assume this is the value of <imath>K</imath>, as the next smallest value of <imath>K</imath> (which is <imath>K=100</imath>) yields the unlikely case that Chloe is currently <imath>101</imath> years old. 

Since <imath>K=36</imath>, we have <imath>C=1+36=37</imath> and <imath>J=2+36=38</imath>. Joey's age is a multiple of Zoe's age when <imath>Z+t|J+t</imath>. Plugging in the values of <imath>Z</imath> and <imath>J</imath>, we get <imath>t+1|t+38</imath>. By the Divisibility of Differences rule, <imath>t+1|t+38-(t+1)=37</imath>. The smallest value of <imath>t</imath> is <imath>36</imath>, so Joey will be <imath>38+36=74</imath> years old. The sum of the digits is <imath>7+4=\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 11}</imath>.
